results.summary: This design implements a motocross racing game for up to four players, each controlling a bike with a single button. It outputs a VGA signal to display the game track and uses bidirectional pins to select among four tracks and set game speed. A reset input restarts gameplay. The design is notable for supporting four simultaneous players with minimal controls and is based on an open-source project.

This design displays either a laboratory logo or an author image on a VGA monitor. It uses input pins to select the image and control color, and outputs standard VGA signals. The design requires only a VGA PMOD board for testing. The documentation is brief and does not provide details on image resolution or color depth.

This analog design implements a voltage-controlled ring oscillator with an 8-bit DAC for frequency tuning. The oscillator frequency can be adjusted either by an external control voltage or by digital input to the DAC. It provides a divided oscillator output for measurement with an Arduino. Testing requires a power supply and oscilloscope, and the design is notable for combining analog and digital control in a compact analog block.

This design is a digital jitter meter that measures timing displacement of an input signal relative to a reference clock up to 50 MHz. It uses a UART interface for configuration and data retrieval, and includes hardware gating to pause measurements. External hardware such as a microcontroller and signal generator are needed for testing. The design is notable for its high-speed capture engine and real-time statistics.

This design implements a multiplier-less exponential-minus-log (EML) gate using Mitchell's approximation for energy-efficient transcendental processing. It communicates via SPI, with pins for MOSI, MISO, SCK, and chip select. The documentation is minimal, providing only the title and pin names, so the exact functionality and testing procedure are unclear. It is likely intended for arithmetic-intensive applications in ASICs.

This design is a finite state machine intended as a replacement for a PCB board in the VAK lab at Northwestern. It interfaces with an ADC, SPI devices such as FRAM and LoRa, and controls power to sensors and radio. The design includes pins for ADC data, SPI communication, and control signals. Testing is planned locally, and no external hardware is required at this moment.

This design receives serial data via UART, stores it in an 8-bit register, and compares it with a pseudo-random pattern generated by an LFSR. When the received byte matches the LFSR pattern, it activates an output signal on an LED. The design can be tested with a UART frame generator and observed via LEDs or a logic analyzer. No external hardware is strictly required for the core logic.

This design generates multiple clock signals by dividing the input clock frequency based on a user-selected module value. It uses an 8-bit input to set the division factor and provides divided outputs on both bidirectional and output pins. The design requires no external hardware and can be tested by setting the module inputs. It is a simple utility for clock management.

This design implements a traffic light controller as a finite state machine, using an instantiated clock frequency divider for timing. It cycles through red, green, and yellow states with durations of 30, 20, and 3 seconds respectively. The design can be tested by setting the start input and observing the outputs, optionally with external LEDs. It is a simple educational example of FSM-based control.

This analog design implements a 1.2V CMOS bandgap voltage reference with a 3-bit resistor trimming network for PVT variation compensation. It uses a beta multiplier amplifier topology with a folded cascode OTA and provides two output nodes for measurement. Testing requires high-impedance measurement equipment to avoid loading the unbuffered outputs. The design is notable for its trimming capability and analog implementation.
